name.text: 01 Content: The IIIF Vision: Solving the Image Silo Problem

questiontext.text:
The IIIF Vision: Solving the Image Silo Problem

Libraries spent decades digitizing manuscripts, and each one built its own website to show them. Every site had its own viewer, its own zoom buttons, its own file formats. You could look at an image, but only in that library's window.

Scholars call this an image silo: the pictures are online, but locked to one portal. To compare a Dickinson poem at Harvard with one at Amherst, you opened two windows that could not talk to each other, or downloaded huge files onto your laptop.

IIIF (the International Image Interoperability Framework, said "triple-eye-eff") fixes this by agreeing on shared rules. Any library that follows them can be read by any viewer that follows them.

Vocabulary. IIIF — shared rules for publishing images so any compliant viewer can read them. Image silo — digitized material viewable only through one institution's own website.

Takeaway: IIIF replaces one-library-one-viewer silos with shared rules, so images from different institutions can be used in the same tool.

name.text: 01 Question: The IIIF Vision: Solving the Image Silo Problem

questiontext.text: What problem was IIIF created to solve?

generalfeedback.text: IIIF replaces one-library-one-viewer silos with shared rules, so images from different institutions can be used in the same tool.

answer.text: Digitized images were locked to each library's own website and viewer, so material from different institutions could not be used together.

feedback.text: Correct. That lock-in is what the lesson calls an image silo, and shared rules are what break it.

answer.text: Libraries had not yet digitized enough manuscripts to make comparison worthwhile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The images existed; the problem was that each institution published them in an incompatible way.

answer.text: Digital images degraded over time and needed a format that would not fade.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital files do not fade; the problem was access and compatibility, not decay.

answer.text: Copyright law prevented scholars from viewing manuscripts held in other countries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF is a technical standard and does not change the rights in an image.

name.text: 02 Content: The IIIF Image API: The Canonical Request URI Syntax

questiontext.text:
The IIIF Image API: The Canonical Request URI Syntax

The first half of IIIF is the Image API. It turns a web address into a request for exactly the piece of the image you want.

Every request follows the same pattern:

{server}/{identifier}/{region}/{size}/{rotation}/{quality}.{format}

Reading it left to right: region is which part of the image (full, or x,y,w,h in pixels), size is how big to send it back (max, or 600, for 600 pixels wide), rotation is degrees clockwise, quality is default, gray, or bitonal, and format is usually jpg.

So .../full/1000,/0/default.jpg means the whole page, 1000 pixels wide, unrotated, in colour. Change one word and you get a different picture — no software required.

Vocabulary. API — an agreed way for one program to ask another for something. Region — the rectangle of the source image being requested.

Takeaway: A IIIF image address is a readable recipe: region, size, rotation, quality, format — so you can crop and resize a page by editing a URL.

name.text: 02 Question: The IIIF Image API: The Canonical Request URI Syntax

questiontext.text: In a IIIF image address, what does the part of the path immediately after the identifier specify?

generalfeedback.text: A IIIF image address is a readable recipe: region, size, rotation, quality, format — so you can crop and resize a page by editing a URL.

answer.text: The region: which rectangle of the source image to return, either `full` or pixel coordinates.

feedback.text: Correct. The order is region, then size, then rotation, then quality and format.

answer.text: The size in pixels of the image that will be returned.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Size comes after region; the two are separate parts of the path.

answer.text: The compression quality, from 1 to 100.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `quality` in IIIF means colour treatment (default, gray, bitonal), and it comes later in the path.

answer.text: The identifier of the manifest the image belongs to.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests belong to the Presentation API; the Image API path describes pixels only.

name.text: 03 Content: Deep Zoom and Image Tiling

questiontext.text:
Deep Zoom and Image Tiling

A good photograph of a large broadside can be 12,000 pixels across and hundreds of megabytes. No browser can load that before showing you anything.

IIIF servers solve it by cutting each image into tiles: small squares, typically 256 or 512 pixels, prepared in advance at several sizes. Together those sizes form a pyramid, with a small version at the top and the full-resolution one at the bottom.

When you zoom, the viewer works out which tiles are on your screen right now and asks only for those. Panning fetches a few more. You feel like you are moving around one enormous photograph, but you are downloading a handful of small ones.

Vocabulary. Tile — one small square piece of a large image. Image pyramid — the same image stored at several resolutions for fast zooming.

Takeaway: Deep zoom works by sending only the small tiles currently on screen, which is why a gigantic manuscript image opens instantly.

name.text: 03 Question: Deep Zoom and Image Tiling

questiontext.text: Why can a browser display a 12,000-pixel-wide manuscript image almost instantly?

generalfeedback.text: Deep zoom works by sending only the small tiles currently on screen, which is why a gigantic manuscript image opens instantly.

answer.text: The server has pre-cut the image into small tiles at several sizes, and the viewer downloads only the tiles currently on screen.

feedback.text: Correct. You are never downloading the whole image, only the few small squares you can actually see.

answer.text: The image is compressed so heavily that the full file is only a few hundred kilobytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The master stays large; tiling avoids sending it rather than shrinking it.

answer.text: The browser downloads the entire image in the background while showing a placeholder.

feedback.text: Incorrect. With tiling there is no need to transfer the whole file at all.

answer.text: Modern connections are fast enough to transfer several hundred megabytes before the page renders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That transfer would be slow and wasteful, which is precisely why tiling exists.

name.text: 04 Content: The Image Information Document (`info.json`)

questiontext.text:
The Image Information Document (`info.json`)

Before a viewer can request tiles, it needs to know what it is dealing with. Every IIIF image service answers that at one address: add /info.json to the image's identifier.

What comes back is a short text file listing the image's real width and height, the tile size the server prefers, and which ready-made sizes it offers.

This matters for your own work. The JPEG you downloaded may be 1,000 pixels wide while the master behind it is 8,000. Your TEI <surface> coordinates describe one specific image, so you need to know which one you measured. info.json is where you check.

https://example.org/iiif/3/manuscript_f01r/info.json

Vocabulary. info.json — the small file describing an image's dimensions and capabilities. Master — the highest-resolution version an institution holds.

Takeaway: Fetch info.json to learn an image's true dimensions, and record which version your coordinates actually describe.

name.text: 04 Question: The Image Information Document (`info.json`)

questiontext.text: Why does `info.json` matter when you are writing TEI `<surface>` coordinates?

generalfeedback.text: Fetch `info.json` to learn an image's true dimensions, and record which version your coordinates actually describe.

answer.text: It reports the true dimensions of the institution's master, which may be far larger than the copy you downloaded and measured.

feedback.text: Correct. Coordinates describe one specific image, so you must know which version yours describe.

answer.text: It contains the rights statement that determines whether you may crop the image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Licence information may appear elsewhere; info.json is technical description.

answer.text: It lists the zones the institution has already defined on the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. info.json describes the image service, not the content of the page.

answer.text: It converts your pixel coordinates into TEI corner attributes automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That conversion is something you or a script must do.

name.text: 05 Content: The IIIF Presentation API: The Shared Canvas Model

questiontext.text:
The IIIF Presentation API: The Shared Canvas Model

The second half of IIIF is the Presentation API, and it handles structure: a book has pages in an order, a letter has a front and a back.

Its central idea is the Canvas. A Canvas is not a picture. It is an empty rectangle with a width and a height, standing for one physical surface — one page, one sheet, one side.

Pictures are then attached to that Canvas. That sounds like a technicality, but it buys something real: an ordinary photograph, an ultraviolet photograph, and a transcription can all be attached to the same Canvas, because they all describe the same physical surface.

The idea should feel familiar. It is the same move TEI makes when it separates <surface> from the <graphic> inside it.

Vocabulary. Canvas — an abstract rectangle standing for one physical surface, to which images and text are attached.

Takeaway: A IIIF Canvas represents the physical surface, not a file, so several images and a transcription can all be anchored to the same page.

name.text: 05 Question: The IIIF Presentation API: The Shared Canvas Model

questiontext.text: What is a IIIF Canvas?

generalfeedback.text: A IIIF Canvas represents the physical surface, not a file, so several images and a transcription can all be anchored to the same page.

answer.text: An abstract rectangle standing for one physical surface, to which images and transcriptions are attached.

feedback.text: Correct. Because the Canvas is not a file, several images of the same page can be anchored to it.

answer.text: The highest-resolution image file an institution holds for a page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the master image; a Canvas is not a file at all.

answer.text: The viewer window in which a manuscript is displayed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Canvas is part of the data model, not part of the interface.

answer.text: A drawing surface on which scholars sketch annotations by hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Annotations are data attached to a Canvas, not freehand drawing.

name.text: 06 Content: Anatomy of a IIIF Manifest: Structure and JSON-LD

questiontext.text:
Anatomy of a IIIF Manifest: Structure and JSON-LD

A Manifest is the file that packages an object for a viewer: its metadata, its Canvases, and the images attached to them. When someone gives you "a IIIF link", it is almost always a Manifest URL.

It is written in JSON, a format of labelled values in braces:

{
  "type": "Manifest",
  "label": { "en": [ "Emily Dickinson, MS Am 1118.3 (338)" ] },
  "items": [
    { "type": "Canvas", "label": { "en": [ "Recto" ] },
      "width": 3200, "height": 4800 }
  ]
}

You will not be writing manifests from scratch. You should be able to open one and read it: what is this object, how many Canvases does it have, what did the institution choose to tell you about it, and what did it leave out.

Vocabulary. Manifest — the file describing one object: its metadata, its Canvases, and their images. JSON — a plain-text format of labelled values.

Takeaway: A Manifest is the package a viewer reads, and being able to open one and see what an institution published (and omitted) is a research skill.

name.text: 06 Question: Anatomy of a IIIF Manifest: Structure and JSON-LD

questiontext.text: Someone sends you 'a IIIF link' for a document. What are you most likely being given, and what should you do with it?

generalfeedback.text: A Manifest is the package a viewer reads, and being able to open one and see what an institution published (and omitted) is a research skill.

answer.text: A Manifest URL, which you can open to see the object's metadata, how many Canvases it has, and what the institution chose to publish.

feedback.text: Correct. Reading a manifest critically — including noticing what is missing — is a research skill.

answer.text: A single JPEG of the first page, which you should download and crop.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A manifest describes the whole object rather than delivering one image.

answer.text: A login page for the institution's reading room booking system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests are public data files, not access controls.

answer.text: A TEI file you can validate against `msdesc.rng`.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests are JSON; TEI is XML, and the two use different schemas.

name.text: 07 Content: Multi-Page Structures: Sequences, Ranges, and Structures

questiontext.text:
Multi-Page Structures: Sequences, Ranges, and Structures

A one-sheet decree needs one or two Canvases. A bound register needs hundreds, and nobody wants to scroll through them.

IIIF handles this with Ranges, listed under a manifest's structures. A Range is a named group of Canvases: "Chapter 4", "Index", "Quire 2". Ranges can sit inside other Ranges, which is how a viewer builds the clickable table of contents down the side of the screen.

Ranges can also record physical structure rather than contents — which leaves belong to which gathering, where a leaf was cut out, which pages were separated when the volume was rebound.

That distinction is worth holding onto: how a document is built and how it is organized are two different descriptions of it, and IIIF keeps both.

Vocabulary. Range — a named group of Canvases. Quire (gathering) — sheets folded and sewn together as one unit of a book.

Takeaway: Ranges group Canvases into a table of contents or into physical gatherings, letting a manifest record both how a book reads and how it was made.

name.text: 07 Question: Multi-Page Structures: Sequences, Ranges, and Structures

questiontext.text: What do IIIF Ranges let a manifest express that a plain list of Canvases cannot?

generalfeedback.text: Ranges group Canvases into a table of contents or into physical gatherings, letting a manifest record both how a book reads and how it was made.

answer.text: Named groupings of Canvases, such as a table of contents or the quires a volume was built from.

feedback.text: Correct. Ranges can record both how a book reads and how it was physically assembled.

answer.text: The pixel dimensions of each page image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dimensions belong to the Canvas and the image service.

answer.text: The licence attached to each individual image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rights information is separate from structural grouping.

answer.text: The order in which pages were digitized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ranges describe intellectual and physical structure, not capture history.

name.text: 08 Content: Interoperable Juxtaposition: Comparing Witnesses in Mirador

questiontext.text:
Interoperable Juxtaposition: Comparing Witnesses in Mirador

Mirador is a free viewer that shows several IIIF objects side by side. You paste in manifest URLs, and each opens in its own panel.

The point is comparison. Two copies of the same printed decree, held in different archives, can sit next to each other on your screen. Lock the panels together and zooming one zooms the other to the same spot.

For a textual scholar this replaces travel. Comparing two witnesses used to mean two trips, or ordering photographs and waiting weeks.

It only works when both institutions publish IIIF. When one does not, you are back to screenshots and guesswork — which is itself a finding worth recording about your own document.

Vocabulary. Mirador — an open-source viewer for comparing IIIF objects side by side. Witness — one surviving copy of a text.

Takeaway: Mirador puts witnesses from different institutions side by side with synchronized zoom, but only when each institution publishes IIIF.

name.text: 08 Question: Interoperable Juxtaposition: Comparing Witnesses in Mirador

questiontext.text: What does Mirador make possible, and what is its precondition?

generalfeedback.text: Mirador puts witnesses from different institutions side by side with synchronized zoom, but only when each institution publishes IIIF.

answer.text: Side-by-side comparison of witnesses from different institutions with synchronized zoom, provided each institution publishes IIIF.

feedback.text: Correct. Where an institution does not publish IIIF, that absence is itself a finding about your document.

answer.text: Automatic collation of two texts, producing a list of variants without human reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mirador displays images; collation is a separate process covered in Module 7.

answer.text: Downloading complete high-resolution images from any library for offline use.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mirador streams tiles and does not override an institution's access terms.

answer.text: Editing and correcting the images held by an institution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Viewers do not alter the institution's files.

name.text: 09 Content: The Open-Source Imperative in Scholarly Imaging

questiontext.text:
The Open-Source Imperative in Scholarly Imaging

From here on this lesson is about tools you run yourself. They are all open source, and that is a scholarly choice rather than a budget one.

Four reasons:

  • You can check it. If your edition says an image was sharpened, another scholar must be able to run the same operation and get the same pixels. A secret algorithm cannot be verified.
  • It lasts. Editions outlive software companies, licence terms, and subscriptions.
  • It scripts. Three hundred pages cannot be adjusted by hand without drift.
  • Anyone can run it. No subscription stands between a student and the evidence.

The working set is small: GIMP for looking and experimenting, ImageMagick for scripted batches, libvips for very large files.

Vocabulary. Open source — software whose code anyone may read, run, and modify. Batch — running the same operation over many files at once.

Takeaway: Scholarly imaging uses open-source tools because a claim about an image is only verifiable if someone else can rerun the exact operation.

name.text: 09 Question: The Open-Source Imperative in Scholarly Imaging

questiontext.text: Why does this course treat open-source imaging tools as a scholarly requirement rather than a budget preference?

generalfeedback.text: Scholarly imaging uses open-source tools because a claim about an image is only verifiable if someone else can rerun the exact operation.

answer.text: A claim about an image is only verifiable if another scholar can rerun the exact operation and get the same pixels.

feedback.text: Correct. A secret algorithm cannot be checked, and an unverifiable image is weak evidence.

answer.text: Open-source tools produce higher-quality images than commercial ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument is about verifiability and durability, not image quality.

answer.text: Commercial software is not permitted in university work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is permitted; the objection is to undocumented, unrepeatable processing.

answer.text: Open-source tools are the only software that can read TIFF files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many programs read TIFF; the issue is transparency of the operations.

name.text: 10 Content: Interactive Editing with GIMP: Manual Adjustments and Layer Inspection

questiontext.text:
Interactive Editing with GIMP: Manual Adjustments and Layer Inspection

GIMP is a free image editor, and in this course it is the place you look before you script. Three things it is good for:

Curves (Colors > Curves) let you drag a line to darken faint ink and lighten stained paper, watching the effect live. When it looks right, you note the numbers and put them in a script.

Channels show the red, green, and blue layers separately. Faded iron-gall ink is often far more legible in the blue channel alone than in the full-colour image. This is free evidence, and it costs one click.

Layer masks let you try a change on part of an image without destroying the original underneath.

Use GIMP to decide what to do. Use a script to actually do it, so the operation is recorded.

Vocabulary. Channel — the red, green, or blue component of a colour image. Layer mask — a stencil controlling where an edit applies.

Takeaway: GIMP is for exploring an image and finding the right settings; the settings you find then go into a script that can be rerun and audited.

name.text: 10 Question: Interactive Editing with GIMP: Manual Adjustments and Layer Inspection

questiontext.text: What role does GIMP play in the workflow this lesson recommends?

generalfeedback.text: GIMP is for exploring an image and finding the right settings; the settings you find then go into a script that can be rerun and audited.

answer.text: It is where you explore an image and find the right settings, which then go into a script that can be rerun and audited.

feedback.text: Correct. Explore interactively, then record the decision as a command.

answer.text: It is the final production tool, because hand-adjusting each page gives the best results.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand-adjusting many pages introduces drift and leaves no record.

answer.text: It converts images into TEI facsimile markup automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GIMP is an image editor; the markup is written or scripted separately.

answer.text: It is used only for cropping, since its other tools are not accurate enough.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its curve and channel tools are exactly what make it useful for inspection.

name.text: 11 Content: Scripting with ImageMagick: Command-Line Batch Automation

questiontext.text:
Scripting with ImageMagick: Command-Line Batch Automation

ImageMagick does image editing from the command line. One command, typed once, can be applied to one file or three hundred.

magick input.tif -quality 85 output.jpg

Operations can be chained, and they run in the order written:

magick page.tif -deskew 40% -level 12%,88% -colorspace Gray out.tif

That single line straightens the page, stretches the contrast, and converts to grey.

The advantage over clicking is not speed. It is that the command is the record. Paste it into your notes and anyone can reproduce your image exactly, including you in December.

Vocabulary. Command line — typing instructions to the computer as text. Chaining — combining several operations in one command.

Takeaway: An ImageMagick command applies identical treatment to every page and doubles as the written record of what was done.

name.text: 11 Question: Scripting with ImageMagick: Command-Line Batch Automation

questiontext.text: Besides speed, what is the scholarly advantage of processing images with an ImageMagick command?

generalfeedback.text: An ImageMagick command applies identical treatment to every page and doubles as the written record of what was done.

answer.text: The command itself is the record of what was done, so anyone can reproduce the result exactly.

feedback.text: Correct. A written command is documentation and instruction at the same time.

answer.text: Commands produce higher-resolution output than graphical editors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution comes from the capture, not from the interface used to process it.

answer.text: Commands avoid any loss of quality, whatever operations are chained.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lossy saves and repeated rotation still cost quality, whatever tool is used.

answer.text: Command-line tools are the only software that can deskew an image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many tools deskew; the advantage here is the auditable record.

name.text: 12 Content: High-Performance Processing with libvips: Memory Efficiency and Tiling

questiontext.text:
High-Performance Processing with libvips: Memory Efficiency and Tiling

ImageMagick usually loads a whole image into memory. For a 100-megapixel photograph of an oversize map, that can exhaust a laptop.

libvips works differently: it streams the image through in narrow strips, so it needs only a fraction of the memory and uses all your processor cores. On very large files it is several times faster.

Its main job here is making the tile pyramids from section 3:

vips dzsave master.tif output_zoom --tile-size 512

You are unlikely to need libvips for a single page. Know that it exists, and that "my computer ran out of memory" has an answer.

Vocabulary. Streaming — processing an image in small pieces instead of loading it whole. Pyramid — the multi-resolution form used for deep zoom.

Takeaway: libvips streams large images in strips, so gigapixel files can be processed and tiled on ordinary hardware.

name.text: 12 Question: High-Performance Processing with libvips: Memory Efficiency and Tiling

questiontext.text: What problem does libvips solve that ImageMagick typically does not?

generalfeedback.text: libvips streams large images in strips, so gigapixel files can be processed and tiled on ordinary hardware.

answer.text: It streams very large images in narrow strips, so gigapixel files can be processed without exhausting memory.

feedback.text: Correct. It is also the standard tool for generating deep-zoom tile pyramids.

answer.text: It corrects colour more accurately than other tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colour correction depends on profiles and targets, not on this tool.

answer.text: It can read formats that ImageMagick cannot open at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The difference is memory handling and speed, not format support.

answer.text: It recovers detail from low-resolution images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No deterministic tool adds detail that was never captured.

name.text: 13 Content: Reproducible Processing: Logging Parameters and Scripting Pipelines

questiontext.text:
Reproducible Processing: Logging Parameters and Scripting Pipelines

Here is the rule that makes the rest of this lesson scholarship rather than photo editing: never change your original, and always write down what you did.

In practice that means three habits:

  1. Keep the original untouched. Downloaded or camera files go in one folder and are never edited in place. Every operation writes a new file.
  2. Put the commands in your repository. A short shell script next to your TEI is better than a memory of which sliders you dragged.
  3. Record the settings with the output. Tool, version, and exact numbers.

You already know why: this is the same argument as your Git commit history from Module 1. Work you cannot retrace is work another scholar cannot check.

Vocabulary. Reproducible — able to be redone by someone else with the same result. Pipeline — a fixed sequence of processing steps.

Takeaway: Keep originals unedited and commit the commands you ran, so every published image can be traced back to the file it came from.

name.text: 13 Question: Reproducible Processing: Logging Parameters and Scripting Pipelines

questiontext.text: Which pair of habits makes image processing reproducible?

generalfeedback.text: Keep originals unedited and commit the commands you ran, so every published image can be traced back to the file it came from.

answer.text: Never edit the original in place, and commit the commands you ran alongside your edition.

feedback.text: Correct. This is the same discipline as your Git history, applied to pixels.

answer.text: Save every intermediate version as a JPEG, and note the date of each.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Repeated JPEG saves lose data, and dates do not record what was done.

answer.text: Use the same software version as your institution, and avoid scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scripts are what make the process repeatable; avoiding them defeats the purpose.

answer.text: Work only in a graphical editor so the changes can be seen as they are made.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Watching a change happen does not record the parameters that produced it.

name.text: 14 Content: Coordinate-Based Cropping: Isolating Folios and Zones

questiontext.text:
Coordinate-Based Cropping: Isolating Folios and Zones

A photograph of a page usually includes things that are not the page: the table, a clip, a ruler. Cropping removes them.

ImageMagick crops by numbers, not by dragging:

magick master.tif -crop 5100x7000+450+600 +repage cropped.tif

That reads: take a rectangle 5100 wide and 7000 tall, starting 450 pixels from the left and 600 from the top.

+repage matters. Without it the file remembers its old size, and viewers can place your cropped image oddly.

Notice that these are the same four numbers as your TEI zone, arranged differently: tools take x, y, width, height, while TEI takes corners. Converting between them is where mistakes happen.

Vocabulary. Crop — cut a rectangle out of an image. Offset — how far the rectangle starts from the top-left corner.

Takeaway: Cropping is specified as x, y, width, height — convert carefully, because TEI's ulx/uly/lrx/lry are corners instead.

name.text: 14 Question: Coordinate-Based Cropping: Isolating Folios and Zones

questiontext.text: A crop is specified as `-crop 5100x7000+450+600`. What do those four numbers mean?

generalfeedback.text: Cropping is specified as x, y, width, height — convert carefully, because TEI's `ulx/uly/lrx/lry` are corners instead.

answer.text: A rectangle 5100 wide and 7000 tall, starting 450 pixels from the left edge and 600 from the top.

feedback.text: Correct. Tools use width, height, and offsets, whereas TEI uses two corners — converting between them is where errors happen.

answer.text: The corners of the rectangle, at (5100, 7000) and (450, 600).

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is TEI's convention, not ImageMagick's.

answer.text: A rectangle 450 wide and 600 tall, positioned at 5100, 7000.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The size comes first and the offsets follow the plus signs.

answer.text: A resize to 5100x7000 followed by a 450-pixel border of 600 pixels' opacity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `-crop` cuts a region; it does not resize or add borders.

name.text: 15 Content: Deskewing and Geometric Alignment: Rectifying Rotational Drift

questiontext.text:
Deskewing and Geometric Alignment: Rectifying Rotational Drift

Pages are rarely photographed perfectly straight. A degree or two of tilt is called skew.

Your eye compensates automatically. Software does not. Skewed lines wander across the rows a computer is trying to read, and a rectangular zone can no longer sit tightly around a tilted column of text.

ImageMagick can measure and correct it:

magick crooked.tif -deskew 40% straight.tif

One caution: rotating an image by a fraction of a degree means every pixel has to be recalculated from its neighbours. Done once at high quality this is harmless. Done repeatedly, it softens fine pen strokes. Straighten once, from the original.

Vocabulary. Skew — unintended rotation of the page in the image. Interpolation — calculating new pixel values when an image is rotated or resized.

Takeaway: Deskewing straightens a tilted page so lines and zones align, but rotate once from the original, because each rotation costs sharpness.

name.text: 15 Question: Deskewing and Geometric Alignment: Rectifying Rotational Drift

questiontext.text: Why should a page be deskewed once, from the original, rather than repeatedly?

generalfeedback.text: Deskewing straightens a tilted page so lines and zones align, but rotate once from the original, because each rotation costs sharpness.

answer.text: Each rotation recalculates every pixel from its neighbours, so repeated rotation gradually softens fine strokes.

feedback.text: Correct. One high-quality rotation from the master is harmless; several accumulate damage.

answer.text: Each rotation permanently changes the file's dimensions in a way that cannot be undone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dimensions can change, but the real cost is loss of sharpness.

answer.text: Deskewing only works correctly the first time it is applied to a file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will run repeatedly; the problem is what repeated resampling costs.

answer.text: Repeated deskewing corrupts the file's embedded metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Metadata loss is a separate concern from resampling.

name.text: 16 Content: Contrast Adjustment and Dynamic Range Optimization

questiontext.text:
Contrast Adjustment and Dynamic Range Optimization

Old documents are often low contrast: ink has faded to brown, paper has darkened to beige, and the two are closer together than they once were.

Contrast adjustment pulls them apart. The tool for thinking about it is the histogram, a chart of how many pixels fall at each brightness. A faded page shows one narrow hump in the middle: no true blacks, no true whites.

magick page.tif -level 15%,85%,1.2 better.tif

Anything below 15% brightness becomes black, anything above 85% becomes white, and the middle is adjusted by 1.2.

The danger is clipping: push too far and faint pen strokes vanish into solid black while watermarks disappear into white. You have not enhanced the evidence, you have deleted it.

Vocabulary. Histogram — a chart of how many pixels have each brightness. Clipping — pushing tones to pure black or white, destroying detail.

Takeaway: Contrast stretching separates faded ink from darkened paper, but over-adjusting deletes the faintest evidence entirely.

name.text: 16 Question: Contrast Adjustment and Dynamic Range Optimization

questiontext.text: What is the danger of pushing contrast adjustment too far on a faded document?

generalfeedback.text: Contrast stretching separates faded ink from darkened paper, but over-adjusting deletes the faintest evidence entirely.

answer.text: Clipping: the faintest strokes are crushed to solid black and features like watermarks are blown out to white, destroying evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. Over-adjustment does not enhance the evidence; it deletes it.

answer.text: The file size grows to the point where it cannot be served on the web.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Contrast adjustment does not meaningfully change file size.

answer.text: The image's colour profile is discarded, so colours can no longer be corrected.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Profiles are handled separately from tonal adjustment.

answer.text: The coordinates of previously defined zones shift.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tonal changes do not move pixels; cropping and rotation do.

name.text: 17 Content: White Balance and Color Calibration: Applying ICC Profiles and Neutral Ramps

questiontext.text:
White Balance and Color Calibration: Applying ICC Profiles and Neutral Ramps

Photograph the same page under a desk lamp and by a window and you get two different colours. The lamp adds yellow; daylight adds blue.

This is a scholarly problem, not an aesthetic one. If your image is yellow, nobody can tell whether the paper aged or your lamp was warm.

White balance fixes it by anchoring to something known to be neutral. Photograph a grey card next to the page, then tell the software that the card is grey; everything else shifts with it.

An ICC profile goes further, correcting a specific camera's colour bias using a printed target of known patches. This is why section 3.1 asked for a colour reference in the frame: it is what makes the correction possible afterwards.

Vocabulary. White balance — correcting a colour cast so neutral things look neutral. ICC profile — a file describing a device's colour behaviour.

Takeaway: Photograph a grey or colour reference with the page, so later viewers can tell ageing from lighting.

name.text: 17 Question: White Balance and Color Calibration: Applying ICC Profiles and Neutral Ramps

questiontext.text: Why is an uncalibrated colour cast a scholarly problem rather than a cosmetic one?

generalfeedback.text: Photograph a grey or colour reference with the page, so later viewers can tell ageing from lighting.

answer.text: A reader cannot tell whether the paper yellowed with age or the lamp was warm, so a claim about the object's colour becomes unverifiable.

feedback.text: Correct. This is why a grey or colour reference belongs in the frame at capture time.

answer.text: Yellow images are harder to compress and produce larger files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colour cast has no meaningful effect on compression.

answer.text: Colour casts prevent text recognition software from running at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recognition may be affected by contrast, but the issue here is evidential.

answer.text: Moodle rejects images that are not in the sRGB colour space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is about scholarly accuracy, not platform requirements.

name.text: 18 Content: Spatial Filtering: Sharpening and Unsharp Masking

questiontext.text:
Spatial Filtering: Sharpening and Unsharp Masking

Every lens softens edges slightly. Careful sharpening restores definition, which matters when you are deciding whether a mark is a punctuation point or a blot.

The standard method is confusingly named unsharp masking: the software blurs a copy, compares it to the original to find the edges, and strengthens those edges.

magick page.tif -unsharp 0x1.0+1.0+0.05 sharper.tif

The numbers control how wide an edge is affected, how strong the effect is, and how much difference is needed before anything is sharpened at all — that last one keeps the paper grain from being sharpened into speckles.

Over-sharpening leaves bright halos around strokes and thickens letters. For palaeography that is damage: it changes what the hand looks like.

Vocabulary. Unsharp masking — sharpening by detecting edges and boosting their contrast. Halo — a bright fringe left by over-sharpening.

Takeaway: Modest sharpening clarifies letterforms; heavy sharpening thickens strokes and misrepresents the hand.

name.text: 18 Question: Spatial Filtering: Sharpening and Unsharp Masking

questiontext.text: What does over-sharpening do to a manuscript image?

generalfeedback.text: Modest sharpening clarifies letterforms; heavy sharpening thickens strokes and misrepresents the hand.

answer.text: It leaves bright halos along strokes and thickens letterforms, misrepresenting the hand.

feedback.text: Correct. For palaeography that is a distortion of the evidence, not just an ugly image.

answer.text: It reveals detail that the lens did not capture.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sharpening boosts edge contrast; it cannot add missing detail.

answer.text: It removes noise from the paper background.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sharpening usually amplifies noise rather than removing it.

answer.text: It converts the image to greyscale as a side effect.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sharpening does not change the colour mode.

name.text: 19 Content: Noise Reduction and Defect Masking

questiontext.text:
Noise Reduction and Defect Masking

Noise comes from two places: the camera (grain in dim reading rooms) and the object (dust, foxing, fibres).

Removing it is tempting and risky. A filter strong enough to erase specks is usually strong enough to erase a faint accent, a hairline stroke, or a point of punctuation.

Choose the gentlest tool that works:

  • A median filter replaces each pixel with the middle value of its neighbours. It removes isolated dust specks and leaves lines alone.
  • Gaussian blur smooths everything, edges included. Rarely right for text.
magick dusty.tif -statistic Median 3x3 clean.tif

The rule: never let the filter be bigger than the smallest mark that carries meaning.

Vocabulary. Noise — unwanted speckle from the sensor or the object. Median filter — a filter that removes specks while preserving edges.

Takeaway: Use the gentlest possible noise filter, because anything that removes dust can also remove the faintest real marks.

name.text: 19 Question: Noise Reduction and Defect Masking

questiontext.text: What rule governs how strong a noise filter may be on a historical document?

generalfeedback.text: Use the gentlest possible noise filter, because anything that removes dust can also remove the faintest real marks.

answer.text: The filter must never be larger than the smallest mark that carries meaning, such as a point of punctuation or an accent.

feedback.text: Correct. Anything strong enough to erase dust is strong enough to erase the faintest real marks.

answer.text: Noise filters should be applied at maximum strength, then the image resharpened.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That sequence destroys fine detail and then fakes its edges back.

answer.text: Noise reduction is safe at any strength because it only affects the background.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Filters cannot tell background speckle from faint ink.

answer.text: Noise filters should be applied only to the archival master, never to derivatives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The master must stay unedited; filtering belongs to derivatives.

name.text: 20 Content: Thresholding and Binarization: From Grayscale to Pure Black and White

questiontext.text:
Thresholding and Binarization: From Grayscale to Pure Black and White

For reading, you want the full-colour image. For handing a page to transcription software, you often want binarization: every pixel forced to black (ink) or white (background).

Doing this well is harder than it sounds. The simple approach picks one brightness cut-off for the whole page, which fails badly on real documents: a shadowed corner turns solid black while faint text in a bright area disappears.

The better approach decides locally, choosing a cut-off for each small neighbourhood based on what is around it. A stained corner is judged against its own surroundings rather than against the whole page.

magick page.tif -colorspace Gray -negate -lat 25x25+10% -negate bw.png

Keep the grey version. Binarization always throws information away.

Vocabulary. Binarization — converting an image to pure black and white. Local threshold — a cut-off calculated separately for each small area.

Takeaway: Local thresholding handles stains and shadows that a single whole-page cut-off ruins, but always keep the greyscale original.

name.text: 20 Question: Thresholding and Binarization: From Grayscale to Pure Black and White

questiontext.text: Why does a single whole-page threshold fail on most historical documents?

generalfeedback.text: Local thresholding handles stains and shadows that a single whole-page cut-off ruins, but always keep the greyscale original.

answer.text: Uneven staining and shading mean one cut-off turns a shadowed corner solid black while erasing faint text elsewhere.

feedback.text: Correct. Calculating a threshold locally, for each small area, handles this properly.

answer.text: Historical inks are brown rather than black, so thresholds cannot be calculated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Brown ink is handled fine; uneven illumination and staining are the problem.

answer.text: Thresholding requires a colour profile, which historical scans rarely include.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binarization works on brightness and does not require a profile.

answer.text: A single threshold makes the file too large for transcription software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binarized files are smaller; the problem is accuracy, not size.

name.text: 21 Content: Masking and Layer Compositing: Isolating Text from Background

questiontext.text:
Masking and Layer Compositing: Isolating Text from Background

Some damage cannot be filtered away. The common case is bleed-through: ink from the back of a thin leaf showing faintly on the front, producing mirror-image ghost text.

The deterministic remedy uses the back of the leaf as evidence. Photograph both sides, flip the back horizontally so it lines up with the front, and use it as a mask — a stencil marking where the ghosts must be. Combining the two mathematically cancels the ghosts while leaving the real text.

magick recto.tif \( verso_flipped.tif -colorspace Gray \) \
  -compose Screen -composite cleaned.tif

The important word is evidence. Nothing is invented here. The ghost is removed because a second photograph proves where it came from — which is exactly the difference between this and the AI methods on Friday.

Vocabulary. Bleed-through — ink from the reverse side showing through the leaf. Compositing — combining images mathematically.

Takeaway: Bleed-through can be cancelled using a photograph of the other side, removing ghosts with evidence rather than guesswork.

name.text: 21 Question: Masking and Layer Compositing: Isolating Text from Background

questiontext.text: In the deterministic method for removing bleed-through, what makes the result defensible?

generalfeedback.text: Bleed-through can be cancelled using a photograph of the other side, removing ghosts with evidence rather than guesswork.

answer.text: A photograph of the other side of the leaf proves where the ghost text came from, so nothing is invented.

feedback.text: Correct. The ghosts are removed using evidence rather than a guess about what lies beneath.

answer.text: The software recognizes which strokes belong to the front and reconstructs the rest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes an inferential method, which is the Friday lesson's territory.

answer.text: The bleed-through is simply brightened until it becomes invisible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would also brighten the genuine faint strokes on the front.

answer.text: The verso is discarded after alignment, leaving only the original file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The verso image is the evidence and should be retained.

name.text: 22 Content: The Taxonomy of Digital Image Formats

questiontext.text:
The Taxonomy of Digital Image Formats

The rest of this lesson is about file formats, because choosing the wrong one destroys evidence permanently.

Four properties tell you what a format can do:

  • Bit depth — how finely tones are recorded. 8-bit gives 256 levels per colour; 16-bit gives tens of thousands, and holds detail in faint ink and dark parchment.
  • Colour space — which range of colours the numbers refer to. sRGB is the safe choice for the web.
  • Compression — lossless shrinks the file and gives every pixel back exactly; lossy makes it much smaller by discarding detail forever.
  • Metadata — whether the file can carry camera settings, dates, and rights inside it.

One principle covers most decisions: preserve in one format, publish in another.

Vocabulary. Bit depth — how many tonal levels a file can store. Lossless / lossy — compression that keeps every pixel, or discards some permanently.

Takeaway: Bit depth, colour space, compression, and metadata decide what a format can carry — preserve in one format and publish in another.

name.text: 22 Question: The Taxonomy of Digital Image Formats

questiontext.text: Which four properties determine whether a file format is suitable for a given stage of your workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Bit depth, colour space, compression, and metadata decide what a format can carry — preserve in one format and publish in another.

answer.text: Bit depth, colour space, compression type, and whether it can carry metadata.

feedback.text: Correct. They lead to one principle: preserve in one format and publish in another.

answer.text: File extension, file size, resolution, and the software that created it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are surface facts rather than the properties that determine suitability.

answer.text: Width, height, aspect ratio, and orientation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those describe the picture's shape, not the format's capabilities.

answer.text: Licence, provenance, checksum, and storage location.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those matter for curation but are not properties of the format.

name.text: 23 Content: TIFF: The Gold Standard for Archival Preservation

questiontext.text:
TIFF: The Gold Standard for Archival Preservation

TIFF is the format archives use for preservation masters, and national digitization standards require it.

Three reasons: its compression is lossless, so the file is identical to what came out of the camera; it supports 16-bit depth, holding gradations that 8-bit formats flatten; and it carries technical metadata inside the file.

The cost is size. A 16-bit TIFF of a large page can run to several hundred megabytes, which is why nobody serves TIFFs to the public. They sit in storage as the authoritative copy, and everything else — the JPEG on the website, the tiles in the viewer — is generated from them.

If you photograph your own document, keep a TIFF or the camera's raw file. Every later decision can be revisited from it.

Vocabulary. Preservation master — the authoritative high-quality file everything else is derived from. Derivative — a smaller copy made for delivery.

Takeaway: TIFF is the preservation master because it is lossless and deep-toned; derivatives for the web are generated from it, never the reverse.

name.text: 23 Question: TIFF: The Gold Standard for Archival Preservation

questiontext.text: Why is TIFF used for preservation masters even though the files are very large?

generalfeedback.text: TIFF is the preservation master because it is lossless and deep-toned; derivatives for the web are generated from it, never the reverse.

answer.text: Its compression is lossless, it supports 16-bit depth, and it carries technical metadata inside the file.

feedback.text: Correct. Web derivatives are then generated from the master, never the other way round.

answer.text: It is the only format that can be opened by every operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Portability is not the argument; fidelity is.

answer.text: It compresses better than JPEG at the same visual quality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TIFF files are much larger; that is the cost of losing nothing.

answer.text: It can be displayed directly by web browsers at any zoom level.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TIFFs are not served to the public; derivatives are.

name.text: 24 Content: Pyramidal TIFF: The Foundation of Local IIIF Servers

questiontext.text:
Pyramidal TIFF: The Foundation of Local IIIF Servers

A plain TIFF is excellent for storage and useless for serving: to send one small tile, the server would have to open the whole file.

A pyramidal TIFF solves this by storing the image at several resolutions inside one file, each already cut into tiles. The server jumps straight to the tile it needs and sends it.

vips tiffsave master.tif pyramid.tif --tile --pyramid --compression deflate

This is what sits behind the IIIF servers from the start of the lesson. The sequence is worth remembering as a whole: photograph the page, keep a TIFF master, generate a pyramidal copy, let a IIIF server publish it, point your TEI <facsimile> at the result.

Vocabulary. Pyramidal TIFF — a TIFF holding several resolutions, pre-cut into tiles for fast serving.

Takeaway: Pyramidal TIFFs let a IIIF server deliver single tiles instantly, bridging archival storage and public zooming.

name.text: 24 Question: Pyramidal TIFF: The Foundation of Local IIIF Servers

questiontext.text: What does a pyramidal TIFF add to an ordinary TIFF?

generalfeedback.text: Pyramidal TIFFs let a IIIF server deliver single tiles instantly, bridging archival storage and public zooming.

answer.text: Several resolutions of the image, already cut into tiles, stored inside one file so a server can send a single tile immediately.

feedback.text: Correct. It is the bridge between archival storage and public deep zoom.

answer.text: Lossy compression, which makes the file small enough to serve over the web.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pyramidal TIFFs remain losslessly compressed.

answer.text: An embedded IIIF manifest describing the object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manifests are separate files in the Presentation API.

answer.text: Automatic deskewing and contrast correction of each tile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Processing happens before tiling and is unrelated to it.

name.text: 25 Content: JPEG: Discrete Cosine Transform and the Cost of Lossy Compression

questiontext.text:
JPEG: Discrete Cosine Transform and the Cost of Lossy Compression

JPEG made photographs practical on the web by throwing data away — deliberately, and permanently.

It works by cutting the image into small blocks and describing each approximately, discarding the fine detail human eyes are least likely to miss. A 100 MB master becomes a 3 MB file that still looks fine.

Two consequences matter for scholarship:

  • The loss is permanent. The discarded detail is gone; saving at higher quality later does not bring it back.
  • The loss accumulates. Every open-edit-save cycle throws away more. Edit the TIFF, export a JPEG at the end.

JPEG is the right format for delivery and the wrong one for preservation.

Vocabulary. Lossy compression — permanently discarding detail to reduce file size. Generation loss — degradation accumulating over repeated saves.

Takeaway: JPEG is ideal for publishing and unacceptable as a master, because its discarded detail never comes back and repeated saving compounds the loss.

name.text: 25 Question: JPEG: Discrete Cosine Transform and the Cost of Lossy Compression

questiontext.text: Why is JPEG unacceptable as an archival master?

generalfeedback.text: JPEG is ideal for publishing and unacceptable as a master, because its discarded detail never comes back and repeated saving compounds the loss.

answer.text: Its compression permanently discards detail, and every re-save discards more.

feedback.text: Correct. Saving at a higher quality later cannot restore what was thrown away.

answer.text: JPEG files cannot store colour profiles or camera metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JPEG can carry both; the objection is the permanent data loss.

answer.text: JPEG images cannot be displayed at high resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JPEGs can be very large; the issue is what compression removes.

answer.text: JPEG is a proprietary format that may stop being supported.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JPEG is an open standard in universal use.

name.text: 26 Content: PNG: Lossless Web Delivery and Alpha Transparency

questiontext.text:
PNG: Lossless Web Delivery and Alpha Transparency

PNG sits between the two: compressed for the web, but lossless. Saving and re-saving costs nothing, which makes it the right choice for anything with hard edges — screenshots, diagrams, charts, and images with text.

Its distinctive feature is transparency. A PNG pixel can be fully transparent, fully opaque, or anywhere between, so non-rectangular things can be shown without a white box around them.

That is useful in editions: a wax seal or an irregular fragment can be displayed against any background, and semi-transparent overlays — for example colour-coding two scribal hands — can sit on top of a page image without hiding it.

PNGs are larger than JPEGs. Use them when edges or transparency matter.

Vocabulary. Transparency (alpha) — per-pixel information about how opaque a pixel is.

Takeaway: PNG is lossless and supports transparency, making it right for diagrams, overlays, and cut-out features like seals.

name.text: 26 Question: PNG: Lossless Web Delivery and Alpha Transparency

questiontext.text: When is PNG the right choice over JPEG?

generalfeedback.text: PNG is lossless and supports transparency, making it right for diagrams, overlays, and cut-out features like seals.

answer.text: When edges must stay crisp or parts of the image must be transparent — diagrams, overlays, and cut-out features such as seals.

feedback.text: Correct. PNG is lossless, so repeated saving costs nothing, at the price of a larger file.

answer.text: Whenever the image will be published, since PNG is always higher quality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. For continuous-tone photographs of pages, JPEG delivers acceptable quality at much smaller size.

answer.text: When the image must carry an embedded colour calibration target.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Targets are photographed; they are not a format feature.

answer.text: When the file must be readable by a IIIF server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF servers work from pyramidal masters and can deliver several formats.

name.text: 27 Content: GIF and Modern Web Formats: WebP, AVIF, and 8-Bit Palettes

questiontext.text:
GIF and Modern Web Formats: WebP, AVIF, and 8-Bit Palettes

GIF is the oldest web image format and the wrong tool here. It allows only 256 colours in an image, so a photograph of a parchment leaf is reduced to a mottled approximation, and its transparency is all-or-nothing, leaving jagged edges.

Two newer formats do better. WebP and AVIF both compress substantially harder than JPEG at the same visible quality, support transparency, and come in lossless versions. On a busy image server that saves real bandwidth.

For your projects, the practical guidance is unchanged: master in TIFF, publish in JPEG or PNG, and treat WebP or AVIF as an optimization for later if a viewer supports them.

Vocabulary. Palette — a limited set of colours an image is restricted to.

Takeaway: GIF's 256-colour palette makes it unsuitable for documents; WebP and AVIF are the modern delivery formats, but JPEG and PNG remain the safe defaults.

name.text: 27 Question: GIF and Modern Web Formats: WebP, AVIF, and 8-Bit Palettes

questiontext.text: Why is GIF unsuitable for reproducing a document?

generalfeedback.text: GIF's 256-colour palette makes it unsuitable for documents; WebP and AVIF are the modern delivery formats, but JPEG and PNG remain the safe defaults.

answer.text: It allows only 256 colours and all-or-nothing transparency, so a photograph of a page becomes a mottled approximation with jagged edges.

feedback.text: Correct. WebP and AVIF are the modern alternatives, though JPEG and PNG remain the safe defaults.

answer.text: It uses lossy compression that discards more data than JPEG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GIF's compression is lossless; its limitation is the colour palette.

answer.text: It cannot be displayed by modern browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GIF is still widely supported; it is simply the wrong tool here.

answer.text: It cannot store images larger than 1000 pixels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such limit; colour depth is the problem.

name.text: 28 Content: PDF as an Archival Wrapper: PDF/A Standards and Pitfalls

questiontext.text:
PDF as an Archival Wrapper: PDF/A Standards and Pitfalls

Archives often hand you a PDF of a whole item. A PDF is not an image format; it is a container that can hold images, text, and fonts together.

Two traps follow. First, PDFs usually compress the images inside them with JPEG, so the page you extract may be markedly worse than the institution's master — always ask whether a better image exists. Second, many library PDFs carry a hidden text layer from automatic recognition, uncorrected. Copy text out of one and you may quietly inherit recognition errors into your edition.

PDF/A is the archival variant, which embeds its fonts and forbids anything that may stop working later. Use it for reports, not as a substitute for image masters.

Vocabulary. Container format — a file holding several kinds of content together. Text layer — invisible machine-read text stored behind a page image.

Takeaway: PDFs recompress images and often hide uncorrected recognition text, so never treat one as your image master or your transcription.

name.text: 28 Question: PDF as an Archival Wrapper: PDF/A Standards and Pitfalls

questiontext.text: An archive sends you a PDF of your document. What are the two traps?

generalfeedback.text: PDFs recompress images and often hide uncorrected recognition text, so never treat one as your image master or your transcription.

answer.text: The images inside are usually recompressed and worse than the institution's master, and a hidden uncorrected text layer may be copied into your edition unnoticed.

feedback.text: Correct. Always ask whether a better image exists, and never treat an automatic text layer as a transcription.

answer.text: PDFs cannot be opened without proprietary software, and they expire after a set period.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDF is an open format and files do not expire.

answer.text: PDFs cannot contain more than one page image, and they discard all metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDFs are multi-page containers and can carry metadata.

answer.text: PDFs store images only in greyscale, and they cannot be cropped.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDFs carry colour images and pages can be extracted.

name.text: 29 Content: The Conversion Pipeline: From Master TIFF to Tiled IIIF Pyramid

questiontext.text:
The Conversion Pipeline: From Master TIFF to Tiled IIIF Pyramid

Here is the whole lesson as one sequence, for a single page:

  1. Keep the master. The camera file or the best download you are entitled to, stored unedited.
  2. Normalize, in one recorded command. Deskew, crop, correct colour, sharpen modestly — written down as a command, not a series of clicks.
  3. Build the pyramid. Produce the tiled version if you are serving the image yourself.
  4. Publish a derivative. A JPEG sized for readers, or a IIIF service.
  5. Point your TEI at it. Your <surface> coordinates must describe the image you published — because cropping and deskewing change every coordinate on the page.

Step 5 is the one students forget. Process the image first, then measure it.

Vocabulary. Normalization — the standard corrections applied to every image in a project.

Takeaway: Process first and measure second: cropping or deskewing an image invalidates every coordinate already written about it.

name.text: 29 Question: The Conversion Pipeline: From Master TIFF to Tiled IIIF Pyramid

questiontext.text: At what point in the pipeline should you measure coordinates for your TEI facsimile?

generalfeedback.text: Process first and measure second: cropping or deskewing an image invalidates every coordinate already written about it.

answer.text: After processing, because cropping and deskewing change every coordinate on the page.

feedback.text: Correct. Process first, then measure the image you actually published.

answer.text: Before processing, so the coordinates describe the untouched master.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Your published image is what readers see, and its coordinates differ from the master's.

answer.text: At either point, since coordinates are stored as fractions of the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI coordinates are absolute values describing one specific image.

answer.text: Only after the image is loaded into a IIIF viewer, which recalculates them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Viewers display coordinates; they do not correct ones written wrongly.

name.text: 30 Content: The Deterministic Contract: Transparent Surrogates in the Digital Edition

questiontext.text:
The Deterministic Contract: Transparent Surrogates in the Digital Edition

Everything in this lesson shares one property. Give these tools the same file and the same numbers and they return the same result, every time, on any machine. That is what deterministic means, and it is why this is Step 2 rather than Step 3.

It matters because your reader is looking at a photograph, not the object. They are trusting that what they see reflects the parchment and not your editing. That trust is only warranted if you can show your work: the original file kept, the commands recorded, the settings published.

Friday introduces tools that do not offer this. An AI can propose zones and redraw damaged letters, but it cannot tell you why, and running it twice may not give the same answer. Today is the baseline you will measure that against.

Vocabulary. Deterministic — always producing the same output from the same input. Surrogate — the digital stand-in for a physical object.

Takeaway: Deterministic tools let a reader verify that an image was corrected rather than altered, which is the standard Friday's AI methods will be measured against.

name.text: 30 Question: The Deterministic Contract: Transparent Surrogates in the Digital Edition

questiontext.text: What does it mean to call the tools in this lesson deterministic, and why does it matter to your reader?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic tools let a reader verify that an image was corrected rather than altered, which is the standard Friday's AI methods will be measured against.

answer.text: The same input and settings always produce the same output, so a reader can verify that an image was corrected rather than altered.

feedback.text: Correct. That verifiability is the standard against which Friday's AI methods will be measured.

answer.text: They run without any human input, so no editorial bias can enter the image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You choose every parameter; determinism means the choices are repeatable, not absent.

answer.text: They never change the pixels of the file they are given.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They change pixels extensively; the point is that the change is exactly repeatable.

answer.text: They guarantee that the resulting image is an accurate record of the object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy depends on capture and judgement; determinism only guarantees repeatability.
